t: Tell Me What Youre Excited About
q: Research confirms that discussing positive experiences with others leads to heightened well-being, more energy, and increased life satisfaction.
The hesitancy to share excitement can spring from several sources. One fear is the possible rejection or criticism of a new idea.
Good leaders recognize the importance of sharing excitement with others and the reluctance of many team members to do so.
The famed writer Virginia Woolf had it right when she wrote, “Pleasure has no relish unless we share it.
Good leaders always add relish to everyone’s excitement. They constantly ask others to share their excitement to the benefit of everyone.

t: Valued Within Exercises
q: It's any exercise that gets students thinking about why their coursework matters (Valued) to them (Within).
The key in looking at these examples is to notice that, in each case, students are being given the task of determining why the work matters. They are thinking their way into Value.
Pose a scenario to your students in which a person from the street walks into the classroom and starts ranting about how your class is pointless.
Within a month or so, students in class will roll their eyes when one of their peers says, I couldn't find one. They'll say things like, C'mon, did you have to be anywhere on time?
I like to use prompts like this for end-of-unit Pop-Up Debates. It helps with content review, public speaking practice, student engagement…and with Valued Within.

t: The Big Lie Of Childhood Trauma
q: Events and incidents out of your control invade your well-ordered peace like the hordes of Cimbri.
Your present mood and disposition also transfer to your students. The more anxious and frustrated you feel, the worse they’ll behave.
Here at SCM we’ve long promoted the benefits of maintaining a professional distance—from students, from the job, and from situations out of your control.
For those who practice the discipline of never getting too invested or deep in the emotive weeds, unexpected events act as a trigger to draw back, run cooler, and breathe deeper.
Yes, the unexpected will still strike at the worst possible time. But it will no longer ruin the moment, let alone your whole day.

t: The Quality of the Conversation Perfectly Reflects the Quality of the Relationship
q: Relationships are enacted through conversations, both deep and shallow.
Without a meaningful conversation as a foundation, those who pursue a relationship with others come off more as stalkers than acquaintances who might become trusted partners.
Once the conversation dies, so does the relationship. Rekindling a conversation that has been ignored or neglected is a herculean task.
Weak or thin relationships are created by muted and superficial conversations. Conversely, sturdy and thick relationships are produced through frequent and meaningful conversations.
What’s the quality and frequency of your conversations with those who matter to you or who might matter one day soon?

t: How Do We Learn by Hector Ruiz Martin 2024
q: This books feels significant. Many books try to cover the breadth of educational science gathered round a theme, a thread that pulls them together.
Not a word is wasted, chapters on aspects of teaching (such as feedback or assessment) taught me as much as whole books on the topics had done.
The nuanced discussions of complex issues. Martin reviewed the science related to key topics and pulled out the key findings (or “best bets” as others have labelled them) with exceptional clarity.
It didn’t rule out the benefits of cooperative learning, instead it made clear that the focus should be on assessing the outcome (individuals learning) and not the product.
It also challenged my prejudices. I have been flamboyantly anti-grades. But the book carefully explained where they are beneficial.
It also wasn’t afraid to tackle the scientific backing of some controversial theories such as growth mindset and grit.
Overall, an outstanding summary of where we are with evidence-based teaching. It should become the go to text.

t: Does Instructional Coaching Have a PR Problem? -pr-problem/
q: What’s often missing is the astonishing level of thinking that goes into the myriad decisions that teachers make on a minute-by-minute basis.
To me the issue is that the kinds of examples of action steps which relate to relatively routine, performative behaviours are over-represented in the majority of coaching illustrations.
Coaching without rehearsal is like teaching your students then not getting them to do any independent practise!
So here's my guilty confession... sometimes I don't get a teacher to do rehearsal (of a 'stand up and perform' nature) during a coaching session (though sometimes I do!).
And yet, more often than not when I drop into that teacher’s next lesson I can see them successfully implementing what we were working on.
An over-simplified representation which doesn’t appear to pay respect to the nuance and complexity of coaching could be seen to be doing the whole thing a disservice.
We need to be less dogmatic about rehearsal and acknowledge that it is a part of the coaching toolkit, and nothing more.

t: Developing Teaching: What YOU Do Matters Less Than What EVERYONE ELSE Does hat-everyone-else-does/
q: When it comes to developing your teaching practice, what you do matters somewhat less than what everyone else does. Such is the interdependence of teachers in a school.
It matters because many of our attempts to help teachers improve ignores this interdependence and assumes that the impact of a teacher’s pedagogy is predominantly due to their skill as a teacher.
Even as the lone innovator, the impact of the teacher’s actions are affected by the behaviour of other teachers in the school, even though their practice may not have changed.
Whatever an individual teacher does, the effect will be contaminated by other teachers’ practice.
The interdependencies are largely invisible and the feedback loops are multiple, which means it isn’t possible to predict how this is going to go. We can only observe and respond.
First, we should caution attributing the effect of a teacher’s actions entirely to the teacher’s skill.
Pedagogical innovation cannot be implemented; it must be allowed to emerge.

t: 3-Read Friday #41: A New Book, Coaching Rehearsal, and Interdependencies
q: I attended some CPD delivered by Doug Lemov last week (#namedrop).
He shared a passage from the book about the importance of building on prior knowledge, and I was hooked, so it is straight on my summer reading list.
The bit that really stood out for me was the section on rehearsal and Paul's confession that sometimes he chooses not to include rehearsal as part of his coaching.
There is plenty to think about for leaders, coaches and coachees here.
When I visit a school to work with their maths department, I always insist on meeting with SLT members at the end of the day to discuss what I have asked colleagues to work on.
It is much easier for a department to make a change if there is support from SLT, but also if other departments might wish to work in the same area.
Matthew's superb post articulates the power of such interdependencies.

t: The Power of Prompts to Reinforce New Behaviors
q: Prompts activate behaviors. Without them, most behaviors and actions would never happen.
Without a reliable prompt, many actions don’t happen or are forgotten. This is especially true when we try to create a new habit.
Existing prompts might be: Any time a colleague repeats their argument or presents the same opinion three times in a row
Another option is to design a brand-new prompt that doesn’t naturally exist.
Small nudges can be powerful aids for creating new patterns of behavior.

t: When Leaders Must Choose the Least Worst Option
q: Decisions, like the one Styron poses, are more complex than no-win or lose-lose situations.
Accepting that the options available are all negative and there is no way to reframe or recast the situation to create a positive choice and outcome is a critical first step.
Applying values, preferred consequences, and long-term versus short-term thinking helps decision-makers to create a hierarchy of pain.

The goal of choosing the least worst option offers a frame from which to act rather than to become paralyzed by the distaste of having to select from a set of choices that are highly flawed or plagued by negative ramifications.
Great leaders are never defined by the easy decisions they make. It is with the hardest of calls that reveals to the world who leaders really are.

t: A Primer on Humility While Touting Achievement
q: If you want people to think well of you, do not speak well of yourself.
Research confirms that people who don’t tell others what they have accomplished or about their favorable results are often overlooked and thought to be less successful than others who do.
The key is to tell others about your setbacks before sharing the achievement.
Being humble without being overly modest is where the best leaders land.
By admitting the struggle before success, humility takes root but avoids the modest silence that too often submarines the notice it takes to advance in the workplace and in life.

t: Organizing Yourself Relationally
q: When leaders think of being highly effective, efficient, and organized, they naturally turn to thoughts of strategy, tasks, and tactics that promote productivity.
Yet, many of the world’s best leaders operate on a track they believe is better than organizing themselves around tasks, processes, and meetings. These leaders organize themselves relationally.
Essentially, leaders who organize themselves relationally replace to-dos or tasks with people.
Maintaining this list is essential, as no one can do this in their head for more than a few dozen relationships.
Relationally organized leaders try never to go more than 90 days without conversing with those they don’t engage with naturally through their work or family life.

t: #67 Be Careful With Questions That Have More Than One Correct Answer
q: So, the teacher needed to process nearly 200 pieces of data in the 5 seconds that her students’ boards were in the air. Impossible.
The teacher did all she could, which was to focus her attention on one or two boards and make assumptions about the understanding of the rest of the class based on this.
She could have been more clear about how she wanted the answer laid out: I want your answers written nice and big, and match each number up with its factor pair, starting with the smallest factor.
Another option is to change the question so there is just one answer.

The key point is that for each of these questions, she would have had a much better chance of seeing all her students' responses because she is now checking 30 pieces of data as opposed to nearly 200.
Of course, questions with multiple answers have a key role to play in the classroom. We just need to think carefully about how we will assess them.

t: Why Team Members Tolerate a Tyrannical Leader
q: a small slice of leaders has developed a harsh and highly coercive style, bordering on cruelty.
Over time, they come to prefer a leader they know to one who they don’t know and who might be worse.
The Stockholm Syndrome is a psychological response to abuse, and it applies as much to leadership as it does to cases of child abuse and hostage situations.

Those with this Syndrome in the leadership space will often deny how badly they are treated and rally to the defense of a leader or coach who they believe pushes them to achieve and brings out the best in them.
Unfortunately for the world, there are far too many tyrannical leaders to go around.

t: When to Remind Team Members They Are Part of Something Bigger Than Themselves
q: Leaders often have to ask team members to sacrifice their self-interest or to accept uncomfortable changes.
While it is good practice to keep the larger purpose or vision that is bigger than any one person consistently in front of the team, it is during periods of change that it is most impactful.
The best leaders save the case for why everyone is a part of something bigger than themselves for when they must ask others to adopt unpopular changes or make short-term sacrifices.
Reminding team members about why they really work so hard and commit to overcoming difficult problems and situations softens any resistance to the need to change or sacrifice.
Greatness in all dimensions is born from sacrifice for the larger good.

t: When Delivering Bad News, Is It Better to Surprise Others or Give Them Advance Notice
q: Leaders who deliver a tough message or bad news have a choice to make.
Surprising people with bad news often creates a quick resolution to the issues involved.
However, surprising others with bad news will often create shock, a feeling of helplessness, or a highly emotional response.
Leaders who tend toward advance notice are rewarded with more rational and constructive conversations with the other party.
advance notice is viewed as more respectful and will usually lower the emotional temperature of the news and the reaction to it.

t: Variety Is the Spice of Math Class
q: I don't have any magical secret to engagement, but I think one big piece is that we do a lot of different types of thinking in a typical math class. That variety gives kids lots of ways to participate.

One risk of having lots of different things happening in class is that it starts to feel chaotic. If I'm always giving directions explaining some new thing kids end up confused and frustrated and not learning very much.

We stick with the same puzzle type on the Do Now every 4-5 weeks. We spend time on them the first few days as kids learn how they work. Then I often don't go over them at all as students become more independent.

For instance, I had one student who hated my Do Nows. He would refuse to take them, and rip up the paper if I gave him one. But he loved Desmos lessons, and would be excited to explore and share his ideas in that context.

Finally, I have to remember that engagement is not the same as learning... If my only goal is engagement I'll end up teaching a bunch of fun but poorly sequenced activities that keep kids busy and happy but don't teach very much.

t: The Best Ways to Use One-Pagers
q: The person who learns the most from a one-pager is the person who makes the one pager.
In other words, you need to do all those generative learning activities that are most likely to ensure that you learn and remember new ideas.
Notice the key here: focused work over time. We don't get the benefit of walkthrus by reading Walkthrus. We get the benefit by choosing one of them and dwelling on it for meaningful periods of time.
This process creates the illusion of understanding; I believe that I have learned something about worked examples.

They DO benefit the people who create them... They DO benefit people who already know a great deal about a topic... But they DON'T benefit beginners who use them as their form invites us to use them: a quick read.

t: Fix Your Curriculum Resources First! (But Not in the Way You Think)
q: In no way do I think that schools should 'fix' their curriculum resources before any other improvement initiative if by 'fix' we mean, 'make state-of-the-art'.
But I do think that schools should 'fix' their curriculum resources at a relatively early stage of an improvement journey where to 'fix' means to 'prescribe, share, and set in place'.

Without curriculum resources fixed in place, teachers end up speaking in generalities. A department member might say, ‘I taught that with a worked example’, ignoring the fact that every other teacher in the department has a different understanding of what that term, ‘worked example’, means.
The point is not to get it completely right the first time, the point is to have a concrete starting point from which to improve.
Having prescriptive and shared curriculum resources is one of the ingredients of high performing schools. Without it, we're adrift in a world world of ambiguity.

t: 3-Read Friday #40: Curriculum Resources, One-Pagers, and Variety in Math Class
q: Ollie and I regularly discuss the pros and cons of centrally planned resources and curricula during our monthly podcast chats.
Here, Ollie outlines his argument for establishing a shared curriculum as soon as possible so we can focus on improving classroom pedagogy.
One-page summaries of key research papers or teaching techniques are everywhere these days.
Andrew shares some ways these one-pagers could be used ineffectively and some strategies to get the most out of them.
It gives you a window into his teaching, emphasising the critical balance between serving students a varied diet of activities and experiences and tapping into the power of consistent routines.

t: Reinforcing a Teams Identity
q: Teams that work together over a long period of time commonly develop an identity distinct from the organization’s culture.
A strong identity breeds confidence and allows the team to stand strong when challenged.
Good leaders listen for this emerging identity and reinforce it.
some leaders take a more strategic approach and promote an identity that doesn’t yet exist.
team identities shape experience and create expectations. How does your team see itself?

t: How And Why Not To Take Misbehavior Personally
q: You need one classroom management approach. Picking and choosing what you like from different methods, books, or philosophies results in surefire failure.
They want three tips or a single video to right the ship. They want someone to hold their hand and walk them through what is clearly written on the page.
Rest assured, the conditions you’re experiencing, no matter how bad they seem, are the same as thousands of other teachers right now.
Here at SCM, we crush excuses underfoot like Goliath of Gath.
You have to throw away the deceptions and doubts, embrace the burden and responsibility, and decide: “I can do this and nothing will stop me.

t: Give Me Some Feedback About My Feedback
q: Feedback is the breakfast of champions.” But not everyone wants to eat that breakfast.
It’s not enough for leaders to simply offer the feedback team members need. Promoting a healthy appetite for feedback is the job of every good leader.
Leaders who are wise enough to ask this question increase the appetite for more feedback in the future.
Asking for feedback about feedback will also reveal issues of accuracy and timeliness.
It often recalibrates the relationship because it reinforces the leader’s positive intent. Just another bonus provided by a simple question.

t: Cautiously Learning From the Success of Former Leaders
q: Many uncontrollable factors play an oversized role in the results organizations and leaders enjoy.
Success is not easily repeatable when conditions change, and they are always changing.
The skills former leaders showcase, the behaviors they employ, and many of the actions they engage in are often highly transferrable to the future.
But the strategy these leaders followed and the decisions they made to achieve success are not.
When it comes to learning from former highly successful CEOs, coaches, and performers, selective learning works best.

t: How Much Discretion Do Your Team Members Have to Execute the Strategy
q: Unfortunately, executing strategy with key processes, tasks, and actions that are highly scripted produces team member engagement that is both mechanical and superficial.
Too much execution rigor without flexibility and team members disengage. Too little constraint or scripting and team members operate without the stability to create replicable results.
They spend the time to articulate what great execution looks like and to make sure everyone understands the guardrails that keep everyone in the same lane.
When team members enjoy the autonomy to improvise how they enact the strategy within a set of guidelines, they execute with passion and enthusiasm and take ownership for outcomes.
Great execution across the enterprise requires finding the right balance between constraint and flexibility.

t: #66 Check Students Are Listening to Each Other
q: Regular readers will know that I am obsessed with the fact that many students are not listening to us as much as we hope they are.
But if students may not listen to us, they almost certainly do not listen to each other.
One of my favourite things to do after a student has answered a question is to ask three other students at random what that student just said. They almost always cannot.
This is clearly a problem from a learning perspective, especially if we base our next teacher move on the assumption everyone has heard what that student said.
It is also not great from a societal perspective as we help breed a cohort of young people who switch off whenever someone else speaks.

The solution is relatively straightforward: regularly check students are listening to each other by asking them to repeat - or build upon - what another student has said, and then hold them to account if they cannot.

t: Starts of Lessons, Problems and Solutions https://curriculumteamleader.wordpress.com/2024/06/11/starts-of-lessons-problems-and-solutions/
q: Starts of lessons set the tone for what follows. But there is potential for various problems in this part of the lesson.
Teachers who are generally good at circulating and checking during the lesson sometimes miss non-completion in the starter (I’m talking about myself as much as anyone else).
There’s tension between sanctioning the late student and getting into an argument or conversation that is going to disrupt the lesson.
It’s better to give a clear expectation that they will complete something than just to let them write the title/date and wait for the lesson to start.
The above should work if you are consistent and firm and your school has a system that sanctions lateness in some way.

t: How to Avoid Focusing on Irrelevant Information When Making a Decision
q: Leaders sometimes think putting all the facts and data on the table will clarify the problem and make an obvious decision clear. It doesn’t. It sometimes makes it worse.
Research has shown that even small amounts of irrelevant or surplus information can derail the ability to make quality decisions.
An important first step is to decide exactly what information is needed. Do this even before embarking on the process of collecting information.
The best decision-makers call out irrelevant facts and information that are raised during discussions and hold a hard line against discussing them.
When it comes to decision-making, what you don’t consider can have as much impact on a decision as what you do.

t: Decomposing Decision-Making, A Cognitive Dimension to Teacher Rehearsal gnitive-dimension-to-teacher-rehearsal/
q: One key mechanism identified is rehearsal which means teachers get to practise performing a new technique or strategy before they get into the classroom and do it for real.
This approach may suffer two problems. Firstly, that we may be confined to rehearsing only the behavioural aspects of teaching, the visible 'moves' that a teacher makes.
One key ingredient is to increase awareness and understanding of the decision-making process itself through decomposition – breaking down a particular situation into a more granular set of decisions.
One of the reasons why simply going to observe another teacher often fails to improve someone's practice is because there isn't the accompanying decomposition of what happened in the classroom.

A recent study by Sims et al (2024) showed that decomposition followed by recomposition may increase the likelihood that teachers can transfer the application of teaching techniques to novel scenarios.

t: Area's Just Times
q: We know that misconceptions don’t actually leave pupil’s heads, even when corrected. They’re notoriously sticky, and require the same, if not more, practice in correcting/avoiding them than it takes to embed them in the first place.
For my year 10s, 'perimeter's add, area's times' has been stickier than a post-it. And I can't blame them. It's pithy, easy to remember, but falls apart quickly.
I think it's important to differentiate between misconceptions and errors. It's not that area isn't times as such, it's just that area's isn't just times.
Of course, the fact that students were successful at this means nothing. It doesn’t actually tell me anything about whether I’ve fixed the misconception, because it’s sticky.
Interestingly, one pupil formed the equation 9x=45+18 and then solved that, which would never have entered my head to do!

t: 3-Read Friday #39: Lesson Starts, Teacher Rehearsal, and Area Misconceptions
q: Another good one from Pete here, addressing a problem common to many of the schools I visit each week: How do you get a consistent good start to lessons?
Issues of lateness and behaviour are addressed, and potential solutions are suggested.
As regular readers will know, I am a recent convert to the importance and power of rehearsal when coaching.
Paul takes this to a new level here, suggesting a framework teachers can use to rehearse their thinking and not just their teacher 'moves'.
Dan delves deep into a way to tackle a misconception students often hold about area - that you just multiply the given lengths.

t: Why You Need To Make One Classroom Management Commitment Right Now uccess/
q: So what is it? It’s to take a break for one minute of silence. Not as a punishment, mind you. It must never be viewed as a negative reaction to behavior.
Slower and deeper breathing triggers the parasympathetic nervous system, which is the body’s calming mechanism.
Some classrooms I enter to observe teachers give me the jitters, like I’ve had too much coffee.
Mid-morning, after lunch, and right before dismissal are especially effective times.
As it becomes a habit it will be something your students look forward to, a calming recalibration to a happier state of mind and body.

t: A Team Exercise to Introduce New Best Practices
q: The best team exercises have a measurable long-term impact on the organization and culture.
The primary instruction for each team member is to create a one-page slide (maximum one side, one page) that explains a Best Practice they believe should be introduced and incorporated.
When the team gathers, each team member takes three minutes or less to persuasively present their Best Practice to the group.
Selecting a champion to make sure each Best Practice becomes a mainstay in the enterprise is also a good idea.
Do this exercise once a year, and over a span of time, you will find more than a dozen new Best Practices that can become part of how the team and organization operate more effectively.

t: How Do You Know If a Job Candidate Has the Passion for the Work
q: Nothing is more frustrating or deflating than investing months and years in training a new colleague for success, only to learn they lack the passion for the work and will seek an opportunity in another discipline elsewhere.

It’s nearly impossible during the recruiting process to discern whether a prospective team member has the passion, commitment, and interest to build their skills and engage in the work of the enterprise over the long term.
Asking prospective team members what they see themselves doing in 5-10 years will often reveal where their true passions lie.
Because prospective hires typically can’t see why an honest answer to the question would cause concern, they are commonly very open in their expression.
When it comes to passion for the work, the fewer misses the better.

t: The Rashomon Effect or the Downside of Being Smart
q: Smart people are more prone to let their biases cloud their thinking.
Known as the Rashomon Effect in cinema, it’s named after a 1950 Japanese film in which four witnesses describe a murder in four contradictory ways.
Rather than deny this sense-making and the biases it contains, great decision-makers seek a second narrative on the same facts and information.
By comparing the competing narratives during the decision-making process, the leader is less likely to be blind to their biases or to allow them to operate unchallenged.
The power of a story to shape meaning should never be taken lightly.

t: #65 Make Invisible Steps Visible
q: One of the many ideas I took from my podcast conversation with Kris Boulton is the idea of overtisation. Put simply, this means making invisible steps visible to our students, especially when they initially encounter an idea.
He made it super-explicit exactly where the denominator, 9, had come from by showing it is the sum of the two parts, 2 and 7.
Now, most teachers would have mentioned this when explaining the answer, but how many would have written it? I am not sure I would have.
What I find interesting about overtisation is that I actively tell students not to do many of the examples above as they are “not the way a mathematician writes”.
In the initial stages of learning a concept, an insistence upon potentially confusing conventions like these is likely to hinder learning.
Those conventions can be introduced later - a process known as covertisation - when shortcuts can be made in the name of both convention and efficiency.

t: Reading for Speed, Backwards
q: Active learners are voracious readers who consume a tremendous amount of information from many sources.
Examine a learner who is not as focused on speed as on efficiency and superior comprehension and you are likely to see someone who does something very odd.
When a reader knows where the author is going, reading the supporting arguments can be accomplished much more quickly without sacrificing comprehension.
Speed is replaced by efficiency in this process and will enable readers to spend the time they believe is necessary to capture the critical ingredients of a book or essay.
when it comes to nonfiction, reading backward is a way to read more.

t: To Get Smarter, Expand Your Inner Circle of Influence
q: Leaders at the top of an organization are notorious for seeking loads of information from many sources, but for trusting only a few key people to help them think through difficult issues and problems.
If two heads are better than one, then 10 heads are a game changer.
People with great experience are commonly delighted to serve as an additional sounding board and source of perspective if they are asked in the right way.
The ultimate recognition for a mentor is to actively include them in the decision process on pressing issues.
Start today to build a personal Board of Directors that reflects a diverse set of viewpoints, experience, and wisdom.

t: Navigating Trade-Offs, Can We Leave Curriculum Behind? lum-behind/
q: Has curriculum had its day, peaked, and troughed? Are we back to the days of pedagogy (and what do we even mean by ‘pedagogy’?) as the be-all and the end-all? Let’s hope not. Because pedagogy should always be in service of curriculum.
Do not make curriculum a trade-off. I repeat: do not make curriculum a trade-off. For to overly (or only) focus on pedagogy is a thoughtless, cloth-eared error.
If the teacher and coach don’t know the content that’s being taught well enough, no instructional coaching – directional or facilitative – will work.
In Making Kids Cleverer, David Didau says that, 'We cannot think with or about something we don't know.'

To know more about a subject’s curriculum doesn’t mean a quick read through the curriculum overview or a cursory scan through the latest subject edu-book lobbed into an Amazon basket. That’s a knowledge chimera, an illusion.

t: Integrity Is Often Reflected by What You Say No To
q: Integrity is easy to see, hard to define, and exceedingly difficult to assess.
Those with integrity say No more often than they say Yes to opportunities, deals, trades, relationships, and many of the other decisions that shape important life outcomes.
They don’t operate on self-interest as much as they do what is right, fair, and honest.
Learning what people say No to and when reveals a lot about who they are, what they truly stand for, and whether they have integrity.

Knowing if others have integrity can prove a nearly impossible task, but understanding when and why people say No to opportunities and relationships can offer some valuable insight. By the way, how often do you say No?

t: Having the Feedback Conversation
q: There will always be Praise, Problem and Action but how these things go will vary quite significantly from teacher to teacher and lesson to lesson.

It adapts to the teacher. If I know the teacher well and have worked with them before, we'll obviously discuss previous feedback and actions but we'll also have shared understanding of some of the problems their facing.
If the teacher reveals an incomplete understanding of the focus area (or a misconception), probe further to make sure you’re clear.

It's worth asking this question even if we have a clear idea of an action that tackles the problem we've defined... the teacher may have a strategy close to what they already do that addresses the problem.

Perhaps controversially, I don't think every solution to every classroom problem can be practiced... Not every improvement a teacher makes will be a practicable behaviour. Some will be shifts in planning, understanding or knowledge.

t: Do Some Students Learn Faster Than Others?
q: The 'astonishing regularity' is that the learning trajectories look almost identical... My claim here isn't that every student learns at exactly the same rate, it's that those rates are more similar than they are different.
Students already knew, on average, about 50% of what the teachers intended to teach!

Using their observations, they could predict with about 80% accuracy which ideas students would learn... Their model didn't take into account any characteristics of the students besides what they observed directly.

I think I can make two claims: differences in student learning speed are minimized when teachers account for prior knowledge of the topic they’re teaching, and differences in student learning speed are minimized when teachers break skills down into small, manageable pieces.
My point is that the differences in learning speed are probably smaller than you think, and if you see big differences there might be some simple ways to help the students who are falling behind.

t: 3-Read Friday #38: Feedback Conversations, Learning Rates, and Curriculum Trade-Offs
q: Those of you who are involved in coaching and lesson observations will enjoy this deep dive into Pete's feedback process.
It highlights - yet again - how little thought I used to put into this key component of teacher development.

One fascinating finding is that the rate at which students learn things is actually pretty consistent, and it is the initial prior knowledge they have of the upcoming topic that makes the difference to the final outcome.
My view from watching 100s of maths lessons over the last few years is that most of the time the curriculum in maths is okay, and it is the pedagogy that needs improving.
But this post from Clare has made me reconsider this. I will be discussing this with Ollie Lovell in our next monthly podcast chat!

t: Could You Report to One or More of Your Team Members
q: In the best of cases, they find themselves as the least skilled people on the team.
How comfortable would the leader be to actually report to one of the existing team members?
When a leader accepts the idea, at least in their head, that they could easily report to a team member, they inadvertently project a respect and admiration for the team that is hard to duplicate.
In cases where a leader is nowhere near accepting such a reporting line, the answer helps to create a blueprint for action about what it would take to get there.

Some questions are worth asking for the impact they have on how we see things. Asking whether you could report to one or more of your existing team members is such a question. Why not ask and learn from it?

t: 2023-2024 School Year in Review
q: Without handling the first two hurdles, there's still too much of a cognitive and motivational barrier to improving the sophistication of student arguments.
The thing with feedback is that with each day that passes between the writing of the piece and getting feedback on it, the student growth return on that feedback decays at an almost exponential rate.
For feedback to be maximally useful, it's more important to make it timely and actionable than it is to make it individualized — hence my tendency to use whole-class feedback.

Giving so much focus and effort to improving our writing led, inevitably, to us improving our writing. Students developed at different rates, with some achieving mastery halfway through the process and some still discovering things from the feedback I gave on the final essays.

t: Leading Team Members Who Retire Before Retiring
q: The dirty secret everyone knows is that some leaders and team members retire before retiring.
Even though they have a tremendous amount to offer, these team members sit on their hands, stay below the radar, and dial back their contributions while they wait until retirement actually occurs.
Promoting more engagement with those who have lost their initiative begins with designing challenging assignments that utilize many of the skills these team members have developed over their careers.
Relocating the team member to a new team, division, or location may be just what they need to start fresh and deliver on the high expectations set by the leader.
The best leaders never accept anything but full engagement, especially from those who have the skills, wisdom, and experience to contribute.

t: Ask Your Leader to Define the Criteria of Success Before Beginning Any Role, Assignment, or Initiative
q: Nothing is more infuriating to team members than reaching the end of an assignment they believe has been successfully completed only to learn the leader is disappointed with the outcome.
Asking a leader to work backward from a successful endpoint, including a careful description of the triumphant finish, creates a very different kind of clarity.
No one can read the mind of a leader to know what they really expect from a role, project, or initiative.
This simple but powerful clarity will often prevent disappointment for both parties at the end of a project or when measuring the effectiveness of a new role.
Avoiding unnecessary distress at the end of an assignment can depend on achieving this clarity. Don’t start a project or accept a new role without it.

t: Framing Challenging Assignments Positively
q: How leaders frame the challenge varies along a continuum from positive to negative, from optimistic to pessimistic, and from encouraging to forewarning.
I have the utmost confidence in you to tackle this assignment. You’ll do great and learn a lot.
They know confidence drives high performance and they go out of their way to provide it.
It is surprising how often leaders think they have been optimistic and encouraging when they have actually delivered a pessimistic and discouraging message.
Framing situations in the positive is a crucially important leadership skill. Practice makes perfect.

t: #64 If You Wrote This, Put Your Boards Down
q: It can be challenging to take in the data of 30 boards in front of you in the few seconds usually allocated for such a check for understanding.
Control the flow of information - ask for the students on the back row to show you their boards first, then the next row, and so on
Reduce the amount of data to be processed - only ask students to show you the final answer or a single step in a solution
In such circumstances, it would be easy to miss an answer or two despite reducing the amount of data to be processed. But the teacher did something smart.
Every time he wrote an answer he could see on his board, he asked any students who had also written that answer to put their boards down.
This further reduced the amount of data to be processed, and meant that he could spot and subsequently address each of the four answers in the room.

t: Leaders Without Character and Strong Values Have No Enemies and Make Poor Decisions

True character lights the path to strong decisions. Accept that you’re going to upset some people and make some enemies. Leadership requires it.
